units.translation: Δαναὸς δὲ πατὴρ καὶ βούλαρχος [Danaus the father and leader of the council]
Danaus the father and leader of the council
to whom it has been commanded to strew the floor of the path with coverings

Thus M: in the copies πετεινῶν [of winged creatures]. The epic form is πετεηνός [winged], the common form πετεινός [winged]: but the old Attic writers seem to have said πετηνός [winged], which form Herodian recognizes in Etym. M. p. 666, 35 and the ship name Πετηνή [Petene] provides in the naval inscription 4b, 66 p. 317. 4c and 36 p. 318 319, to be compared with Πετομένη [Petomene], which is the name of another ship there p. 319 and 481. About which I have spoken in Thes. vol. 6 p. 1013.

I restored it for ὄρνισι [birds], because all the trimeters of this song in strophe and antistrophe are composed of pure iambs. The grammarians have noted that Hesiod used this word instead of the usual πετεινός [winged], about which Lobeck had no reason to doubt, Paralip. p. 159. The grammarians also mention the monosyllabic form πτήν [winged].
I do not refuse to become a meal for winged creatures

It differs from πέτρος [a stone] in that πέτρος [a stone] signifies a stone of larger mass, which can be moved by hands or machines, and is rarely used for πέτρα [a rock], which signifies a rock or crag that cannot be moved except perhaps by a Cyclops or the Hundred-Handers hurling down mountain peaks. Therefore πετρῶν [of stones] is wrongly written for πέτρων [of rocks] in M at Sept. 673.
you will guard this joyless rock
the echo of the island rock resounded
a certain Scylla dwelling among the rocks
there is a rock named after it and the hill of Ares
and a rocky embrace will carry you
Thus also Eur. Cycl. 72 and Μακρὰς πετρηρεφείς [long rock-roofed] Ion. 1400.

[κνημίδας, αἰχμὴν καὶ πέτρων προβλήματα [greaves, spear, and defenses of stones]. Thus I wrote for πετρῶν [of stones], which is in M. In many copies it is πτερών [of wings]. Thomas Mag. explains both: γράφεται καὶ πτερῶν [it is also written of wings], and you might say πέτρων [of stones] thus: the defenses of stones, that is, the shield, which we hold before our body and by which we receive the stones coming at us from our enemies; but πτερῶν [of wings], understand the defenses as arrows. Thus from the copy for αἰχμῆς [of the spear]]
for many were struck with stones from their hands
with a shower of round stones
